catalog_quote: Ɓa, Lua, Tun, and Bolgo have tone systems with three contrastive heights (Low, Mid, and High), with frequent contour tones (e.g. L͡H H͡M, M͡L, etc.), not restricted to long vowels. Tone may have both a lexical and a grammatical function. An illustration of the former is given for Tun (10): (10) Tun (Palayer: 1975: 182) Level tones LL lùù ‘white clay’ sàm ‘madness’ MM tūū ‘pestle’ sām ‘fermented drink’ HH súú ‘story, tale’ Rising tones LM gùū ‘refuse, waste’ mùl ̄ ‘kind of bird’ LH lùú ‘Parinari sp.’ (tree) mùl ́ ‘kind of ant’ MH sṵ̄ṵ́ ‘caterpillar’ lūń ‘kind of skin disease’ Falling tones ML jāà ‘who’ tēǹ ‘shea butter tree’ HM ɓáā ‘speech’ cén̄ ‘hippo’ ... [§5.5] Lua, Tun, and Ɓa have three contrastive tones while Kulaal has only two. ... In this respect one should note that Tun does not reveal any flat H or HH pattern among its reflexes in this table (in particular the Tun reflex of *H is M). Indeed Palayer (1975: 183) underlines that both CV́ V́ and CV́ (V́)CV́ are infrequent in lexical units, except ideophones.

HH súú 'story, tale'' plus rising LM/LH/MH and falling ML/HM sets -- verbatim as quoted (ellipses only). §5.5 (the text layerHAL pp.27-28): 'Lua, Tun, and Ɓa have three contrastive tones whil…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tunia is described as a three-level tone language (L, M, H, plus contours on any syllable) with lexical and grammatical tone; no accessible source states where word stress falls or whether stress exists. The only mention of 'stress' anywhere is Boyeldieu 2020:300, which speculates that Tun object (post-verbal) vs possessive (pre-nominal) pronoun vowel variants reflect 'a difference of resulting syllable stress', without saying which position is stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: H tone rarely forms a plain word pattern (CV́V́, CV́(V́)CV́) except in ideophones (Palayer 1975:183 apud Boyeldieu et al. 2018).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern lexical items (citation forms) and verb tone-class alternations; the pronoun 'syllable stress' remark in Boyeldieu 2020 concerns clitic position within verb+object vs possessive+noun groups.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources use 'Tun (tǔn)', 'Tounia', 'Tunya' for the same language, Glottolog tuni1251 / ISO tug (Riverine Bua, Moyen-Chari, Chad); Palayer's 1975 data are from the Tounia of the Sarh area. No dialect split is described.

sources.note: Passing mention only, p.300 §3.2 (Tun): object vs possessive pronoun vowel variants (o/ə, u/ə) 'are probably explained by their position regarding the governing lexical unit — following the verb (object) but preceding the noun (possessive) — and a difference of resulting syllable stress.' No rule for where stress falls.
